Project Name

Ostsee Rising: a coal mine learns to swim

High-Level Project Summary

Ostsee Rising is an open-source, interactive web app that uses radar from NASA-ISRO NISAR and ESA Sentinel-1 to show a former coal mine near Cottbus, Germany, turning into the country's largest mine lake: the Cottbuser Ostsee. It tracks 94 satellite passes from 2019 to 2026, measures the lake's area on every pass and checks itself against the mine operator's official measurements.

Visitors fly in from a globe, follow a 7-chapter story, and then explore with their own tools: a time slider, before/after swipe, water and plant views, a Dance Map that explains how every spot changed, and Shoreline Watch, which maps where the water edge moved.

Why it matters: after the coal phase-out, the Spree river could carry up to 75% less water in dry summers, and mine lakes are becoming the region's water storage. Their loose-fill shores can also collapse. Radar sees every lake every 12 days, through clouds and at night, for free.

Detailed Project Description

We are four students at BTU Cottbus, and the Cottbuser Ostsee is on our doorstep. Ostsee Rising lets anyone watch, measure and question its transformation from coal mine to lake, using radar that sees through clouds and at night.

What it does

  • Globe intro: scroll from Earth down to the lake.
  • Story (7 chapters): the mine, the slow drought years, the winter the lake doubled, six years in one map, NISAR taking over, why it matters, and an honest chapter on our errors.
  • Time slider and area chart: all 94 passes (2019 to 2026), with the operator's official measurements as reference points.
  • Water view and plant view: co-polarization (VV/HH) shows calm water as dark. Plant view paints the cross-polarization share (VH/VV, HV/HH) green, where leaves scatter the signal.
  • Compare: swipe, fade or spy lens between any two dates.
  • Water history map: the year each spot first went under water.
  • Dance Map: sorts every pixel by how it behaved over all passes (dark from day one, flooded and stayed, flickers, was water but isn't now) and explains the likely physical driver when you click a spot.
  • Shoreline Watch: maps where the water edge moved between any two passes, with area gained and lost in km².
  • Click any spot: its radar history in both polarizations.
  • Share and export: links that reopen the exact view, and a timelapse GIF.

How it works

  1. Data: 77 Sentinel-1 C-band passes (VV and VH, Jan 2019 to Mar 2025), terrain-corrected with NASA ASF HyP3. 17 NISAR L-band GCOV passes (HH and HV, Oct 2025 to Oct 2026), read from NASA Earthdata; the 8 pre-calibration (beta) passes are labelled in the app.
  2. Pipeline (Python): crop to the lake, resample to a 20 m grid, reduce speckle, learn a water threshold from the OpenStreetMap lake outline, classify water using both polarizations, and measure the lake area. Passes that see less than 98% of the lake are skipped.
  3. Export: each pass becomes map-ready images plus one data file the website reads.
  4. Web app: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Leaflet, Chart.js, globe.gl). The Dance Map, Shoreline Watch and plant view are computed in the browser from the radar pixels.
  5. Quality: a safety check runs before every deploy and blocks a broken version from going live. An 88-check browser test suite ran throughout development.

Our water detector agrees with the OpenStreetMap lake outline on 92.3% (Sentinel-1) and 92.9% (NISAR) of pixels. As an independent check, the Dance Map and Shoreline Watch found the lake's 16-hectare floating solar park, built in 2024, without being told it exists.

Physical drivers we found

  • Rain: after the wet autumn of 2023 the separate basins merged and the measured lake doubled in five weeks, from 7.4 to 15.4 km² (Dec 2023 to Jan 2024).
  • Sand: smooth, flat sand reflects radar away like water, which is why we over-count in the early years.
  • Wind: wind roughens the water so it turns bright, causing dips on single dates.
  • Calibration: NISAR's beta passes read higher (up to 20.4 km²) than its calibrated ones (median 17.6 km²).

Who it helps

After the coal phase-out, the Spree could carry up to 75% less water in dry summers, and mine lakes are becoming the region's water storage. Their shores are built from loose fill: a bank at Nachterstedt slid into a mine lake in 2009, and the Ostsee's own dam slipped in 2022 and 2023. Ostsee Rising gives water managers, the mine-rehabilitation company (LMBV), the city and researchers a free, independent measurement every 12 days, and a "look here first" map between survey flights. Nothing in the method is specific to Cottbus: another lake only needs a new name and map box.

What we hope to achieve next

  • Monitor all 23 mine lakes of the Lusatian Lake District, starting with lakes that are still filling (Altdöberner See, Klinger See).
  • Use NISAR interferometry to measure centimetre-scale ground movement on dams and banks.
  • Map soil moisture on rehabilitated land, and the new Rhineland mine lakes after 2030.

Tools

Python (asf_search, hyp3_sdk, earthaccess, h5py, rasterio, pyproj, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, Shapely); JavaScript (Leaflet, Chart.js, globe.gl, gifenc); GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions; Playwright for testing; ffmpeg for the demo video.
